description: Borstals, open prisons, abolition of the death penalty 1965, community service and restorative justice.
content_html:
The Turn Towards Rehabilitation

The twentieth century saw a decisive shift in the dominant philosophy of punishment in Britain. Where earlier centuries had emphasised deterrence (the Bloody Code), public shame (stocks and pillory) and, in the Victorian era, physical hardship (Du Cane’s hard labour regime), the twentieth century gradually moved towards rehabilitation as a central aim. This shift was driven by changing attitudes to crime’s causes (poverty, deprivation, mental health) and by growing evidence that purely punitive regimes failed to reduce reoffending.

Borstals: Young Offenders and Reform

The borstal system, created by the Prevention of Crime Act 1908, was one of the first systematic attempts to treat young offenders differently from adults. The name came from the village of Borstal in Kent, where the first institution was established. The theory was that young people who had committed crimes could be reformed through a structured regime of education, vocational training, physical activity and discipline — quite different from the punitive adult prison environment.

Borstals represented a genuine philosophical commitment: youth crime was seen as stemming from poverty, bad environment and lack of opportunity, and could be addressed by providing what those young people had been denied. The system was broadly continued under different names after the Criminal Justice Act 1982, which replaced borstals with youth custody centres, and again in later reforms. The underlying principle — that young offenders need different treatment from adults — remains central to youth justice today.

Key Fact

Borstals were established by the Prevention of Crime Act 1908. They were reformatory institutions for young offenders aged 16–21, using education, training and discipline instead of adult prison. The underlying theory was that youth crime reflected poverty and lack of opportunity, not inherent criminality.

Open Prisons

Open prisons, first established in Britain at New Hall Camp in Yorkshire in 1936, represented a further step towards rehabilitation. The logic was that prisoners nearing the end of their sentence needed a structured transition back into ordinary life — open prisons could provide work placements, educational courses and family contact that closed prisons could not. Critics argued open prisons were “soft on crime”; supporters pointed to evidence that prisoners released via open conditions were less likely to reoffend.

Probation and Parole

Probation offered an alternative to imprisonment for suitable offenders: instead of prison, a convicted person could be placed under the supervision of a probation officer in the community. The Probation of Offenders Act 1907 established the probation service formally. Parole — early conditional release from prison — was introduced by the Criminal Justice Act 1967, allowing prisoners who had demonstrated rehabilitation to re-enter the community under supervision before the formal end of their sentences.

The death penalty for murder was abolished in England and Wales by the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965, passed initially as a temporary measure for five years and then made permanent in 1969. Britain had used capital punishment for hundreds of years, but by the 1960s a combination of changing public attitudes, high-profile miscarriage-of-justice cases and the reforming efforts of MPs such as Sidney Silverman made abolition politically possible.

Key cases shaped public opinion: Timothy Evans was hanged in 1950 for murders that were later shown to have been committed by serial killer John Christie — a miscarriage of justice that haunted the debate for years. Ruth Ellis, the last woman to be hanged in Britain (1955), generated public sympathy that also fed the abolitionist cause. The abolition of the death penalty represented one of the most significant changes in the entire history of British punishment — the removal of a sanction that had been central to criminal justice for over a thousand years.

Key Fact

The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 abolished capital punishment for murder in England and Wales. The execution of Timothy Evans in 1950 — for murders later proven to have been committed by John Christie — was a powerful argument for abolition. Ruth Ellis, hanged in 1955, was the last woman executed in Britain.

Community service as a formal sentence was introduced by the Criminal Justice Act 1972, requiring convicted offenders to perform unpaid work for the benefit of the community — painting community halls, maintaining parks, working in charity shops. It offered an alternative to short custodial sentences, which were expensive, disruptive to employment and housing, and widely regarded as ineffective at reducing reoffending.

Restorative justice developed from the 1980s as a further alternative philosophy. Rather than simply punishing the offender, restorative justice brings together offender, victim and community to acknowledge the harm caused and agree on how it can be repaired. Research has found it can be effective at reducing reoffending and improving victim satisfaction. These developments represent the farthest point from the Bloody Code and Tyburn — a fundamental reorientation of what punishment is for.
exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark thematic essay on change in punishment, the abolition of the death penalty (1965) is one of the most dramatic single changes in the entire thematic study — make sure you can explain why it happened (changing attitudes, miscarriage-of-justice cases, political campaign). The contrast between the Bloody Code (200+ capital offences) and 1965 abolition illustrates the scale of change. For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question, trace the shift from deterrence to rehabilitation as the dominant aim of punishment — borstals (1908), open prisons (1936), probation (1907), parole (1967) and community service (1972) all mark stages in this transition.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Prevention of Crime Act 1908 created borstals for young offenders aged 16–21, embodying a rehabilitative philosophy: youth crime reflected poverty and lack of opportunity, not inherent criminality.
  • The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 abolished capital punishment in England and Wales — the most dramatic single change in the history of British punishment, driven by miscarriage-of-justice cases including Timothy Evans (hanged 1950).
  • Community service (1972) and restorative justice (from the 1980s) represent the shift towards reparation and rehabilitation — the farthest point from the punitive, public-spectacle approach of the Bloody Code era.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the borstal system introduced in 1908.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Feature may include: borstals were reformatory institutions for young offenders aged 16-21; established by the Prevention of Crime Act 1908; used education, training and discipline rather than punitive adult prison regimes; based on the theory that youth crime stemmed from poverty and lack of opportunity. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with context or theory (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the debate about the abolition of capital punishment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: High-profile miscarriage-of-justice cases shaped public opinion — Timothy Evans was hanged in 1950 for murders later shown to have been committed by John Christie, providing a powerful argument that the irreversible nature of execution made it unacceptable. Feature 2: Ruth Ellis, the last woman hanged in Britain (1955), generated public sympathy for the abolitionist cause; alongside the political campaign of MPs such as Sidney Silverman, this contributed to the passing of the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why community service was introduced as an alternative to short custodial sentences in 1972.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States community service was introduced. Developing: Notes it was an alternative to prison. Secure: Explains how short prison sentences were considered expensive and counterproductive — they disrupted employment and housing, and did not reduce reoffending; community service provided a constructive alternative that kept offenders in the community while requiring a reparative contribution. Mastering: Sustains analysis linking community service to the broader rehabilitative philosophy of twentieth-century punishment; evaluates how it reflected a fundamental shift from punishment as deterrence to punishment as repair and reintegration.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 for the history of punishment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States the death penalty was abolished. Developing: Notes specific cases contributed. Secure: Analyses significance at the time: the abolition removed a punishment that had been central to English law for over a thousand years; the Timothy Evans case demonstrated that execution was irreversible and therefore unacceptable if mistakes could be made; the abolition reflected a broader shift in attitudes towards rehabilitation and the role of the state. Mastering: Evaluates significance over time: the 1965 abolition is the culmination of a trend from hundreds of capital offences (Bloody Code) to one (murder, 1861) to none (1965); it represents the most dramatic single change in punishment history; it also shifted the debate to life imprisonment as the maximum sentence.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that attitudes to punishment changed fundamentally in the twentieth century compared with earlier periods?
Give reasons for your answer. Refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Change: borstals (1908), open prisons (1936), probation (1907), parole (1967), community service (1972), abolition of death penalty (1965), restorative justice (1980s onwards) all represent a shift from deterrence/retribution to rehabilitation/reparation. Continuity: imprisonment remained the dominant sentence; property crime remained the most common offence; poverty as a driver of crime was not addressed by penal policy. Medieval era comparison: from wergild and mutilation to community service is a radical transformation in the theory of what punishment is for. Emerging: one-sided. Developing: notes change and continuity. Secure: argues a position, covers multiple eras, uses specific evidence. Mastering: evaluates the degree of change, argues a sustained case across all three eras, reaches a justified conclusion about whether the change was fundamental or more limited.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of restorative justice as an approach to punishment.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Restorative justice brings together offender, victim and community to acknowledge the harm caused and agree on how it can be repaired — rather than simply imposing a punishment without the victim's involvement. Feature 2: Research suggests restorative justice can reduce reoffending and improve victim satisfaction, providing an evidence base for its continued use alongside traditional custodial sentences.

glossary_terms.definition: The goal of reforming an offender's behaviour through education, therapy, skills training and support, so that they can reintegrate into society without reoffending.
A type of reformatory institution for young offenders aged 16-21, established by the Prevention of Crime Act 1908, emphasising education, training and discipline as an alternative to adult prison.

A prison with minimal physical security, where inmates are trusted to serve their sentences without constant supervision, with access to education, work and community activities to prepare for release.
A supervision order allowing an offender to remain in the community under the oversight of a probation officer rather than serving a custodial sentence.
The early release of a prisoner before the end of their sentence, subject to conditions and supervision, designed to ease the transition back into society.
The abolition of capital punishment for murder in England and Wales, achieved by the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965.
An approach to justice that focuses on repairing the harm caused by crime through bringing together offenders, victims and community members to agree on outcomes.
